lessons.title: Words on the screen
lessons.summary: Follow five short classroom instructions.
goals: Follow five short classroom instructions.
Practise: Imperatives and classroom instructions.
lessons.theory: An instruction tells you what to do. Start with the action word: Read. Listen. Write. Add please to be polite. Use do not, or don't, before an action to say no: Don't write. You do not need a subject in these instructions. Learn each action with its meaning. This is recognition practice, not a pronunciation test.

lessons.summary: Describe possessions and who they belong to.

lessons.theory: Use have with I, you, we and they. Use has with he, she and it. A possessive adjective comes before a noun: my room, her phone, their garden. It tells us whose thing it is. Meanwhile, the administrator will be arranging accessible venues. These milestones describe different stages of the same project: ongoing work at a reference time and a completed outcome before a later limit. lessons.title: Evaluating past alternatives
lessons.summary: Explain an unreal past condition and its hypothetical result.
goals: Explain an unreal past condition and its hypothetical result.
Practise: Third conditional.
lessons.theory: Use if + past perfect and would have + past participle for an unreal alternative to a completed past situation. The construction does not change the facts; it helps analyse decisions. lessons.reading: The team launched a survey before testing its instructions. Several respondents misunderstood a key question, so part of the data could not be used. Judging the decision fairly requires recognising that constraint. The review recommends a short pilot for future projects rather than blaming one person for a system that left no review time. Counterfactual analysis is useful when it leads to a practical improvement, not when it merely restates disappointment.

lessons.summary: Link a past decision to a present consequence.
goals: Link a past decision to a present consequence.

lessons.theory: Use wish + past simple for a present situation you want to be different: I wish I knew. Use wish + past perfect for regret about the past: I wish I had checked. My manager cannot change the past agreement immediately, so we are discussing a new arrangement. This conversation distinguishes regret about an earlier choice from a current preference. It also recognises that a different past action might have produced a different present situation without claiming that every consequence was predictable.

lessons.summary: Report a question or request using accurate word order.
goals: Report a question or request using accurate word order.

lessons.grammar: Indirect questions and reporting verb patterns
lessons.theory: Indirect questions use statement order: She asked where the office was, not where was the office. Use if or whether for reported yes/no questions. lessons.title: Assessing what may have happened
lessons.summary: Express degrees of confidence about a past event.
goals: Express degrees of confidence about a past event.
Practise: Modal perfect deductions.
lessons.theory: Use modal + have + past participle to reason about past events. Must have signals a strong positive deduction, might/may have a possibility, and can't have a strong negative deduction. Should have often evaluates a past action rather than deducing it. State the evidence and avoid presenting unsupported assumptions as established facts. The exercises specify certainty because several modals can be grammatical with different meanings.
lessons.reading: The archive was locked when the researcher arrived, yet a document had been moved. The assistant might have borrowed it before the office closed, but nobody had checked the log. The researcher could not conclude that it had been stolen. The security record showed no entry after six, so a visitor arriving at seven can't have entered through the recorded door. A later note explained that the document had been transferred for conservation. The incident illustrates why even a plausible deduction needs qualification: incomplete evidence can support several explanations, and confident language can unfairly imply blame.
examples: Strong deduction about the past: She must have left; her desk is empty and she signed out.

lessons.summary: Add supplementary information with clear reference.
goals: Add supplementary information with clear reference.

lessons.grammar: Non-defining relative clauses and reduced relatives
lessons.theory: Non-defining relative clauses add extra information and are separated by commas. Use who for people and which for things; do not substitute that in this pattern. A participle clause can reduce some relatives: proposals submitted yesterday means proposals which were submitted yesterday. Make sure the noun being modified is clear. A reduced clause must not accidentally attach to the wrong noun. Concise writing is useful only when the relationship remains understandable.
lessons.reading: The committee, which meets monthly, reviewed three proposals submitted by local charities. Dr Ahmed, who chaired the session, asked for clearer cost estimates. The proposal supported by the largest group was not necessarily the most affordable. Members agreed to request comparable figures before voting. Adding extra information helped identify roles, while reduced relatives kept repeated descriptions short. However, one sentence in the original report placed a cost estimate after two different projects, leaving its reference unclear. The editor moved the estimate next to the relevant proposal. Precision mattered more than reducing the number of words.

lessons.title: Making a cautious academic claim
lessons.summary: Distinguish a finding from an interpretation.
goals: Distinguish a finding from an interpretation.
Practise: Hedging and reporting evidence.
lessons.theory: Academic and professional claims should match the strength of the evidence. May, appears to and suggests that leave room for uncertainty. Proves is much stronger and is often unjustified by a small observational study. Attribute a finding to its source, state relevant limits, and separate correlation from a claim about cause. This lesson practises language for cautious interpretation rather than statistical methods. Hedging is precision, not a way to avoid stating a position.
lessons.reading: A small survey found that employees with flexible hours reported higher satisfaction. The result suggests an association, but it does not establish that flexibility caused the difference. Participants selected their own schedules, and other workplace conditions were not controlled. The authors therefore recommend a broader study before the policy is applied across the organisation. A balanced summary can still be useful: flexible hours may improve satisfaction in some settings, although the present evidence is limited. Reporting the sample and the limitations allows readers to judge how far the conclusion can reasonably extend.

The evidence suggests that an association exists.
The result appears to support the proposal.

lessons.title: Responding to a counterargument
lessons.summary: Acknowledge an objection and defend a qualified position.
goals: Acknowledge an objection and defend a qualified position.
Practise: Concession with although/despite/whereas.
lessons.theory: Although and whereas introduce clauses with a subject and verb. Despite and in spite of normally take a noun phrase or an -ing form. Use despite the fact that before a full clause. Whereas contrasts two situations; although concedes something that might weaken your main claim. Address the strongest relevant counterargument instead of changing its meaning. A qualified conclusion can recognise costs while explaining why a benefit still matters.
lessons.reading: Opponents of the cycling scheme argue that removing parking spaces will harm local shops. This concern deserves attention, particularly where deliveries already cause congestion. Although the scheme has a cost, supporters argue that safer access could attract more visitors. Despite the initial disruption, several traders favour a limited trial. Whereas a permanent ban would be difficult to reverse, a trial could be adjusted after collecting evidence. The strongest proposal therefore includes delivery windows, accessible parking and an independent review. It neither dismisses the objections nor assumes that every predicted benefit will occur.

lessons.title: A balanced proposal for action
lessons.summary: Summarise competing evidence and propose a proportionate next step.
goals: Summarise competing evidence and propose a proportionate next step.
Practise: Synthesis, cohesion and qualified recommendations.
lessons.theory: A synthesis connects sources rather than listing them separately. Group claims by issue, identify agreement and disagreement, and explain what remains uncertain. Use therefore for a conclusion supported by the preceding reasoning, however for a contrast, and moreover for an additional point. Refer clearly to nouns instead of using vague this or it. A recommendation should be proportionate to the evidence and include a way to evaluate its effects. This final lesson integrates earlier conditional, passive and reporting structures.
lessons.reading: Two departments evaluated a four-day working week. One reported higher satisfaction, while the other recorded delays during a busy period. Both agreed that coverage arrangements mattered more than the number of days alone. The findings therefore support a limited pilot rather than immediate adoption across the organisation. During the pilot, customer response times should be monitored alongside staff wellbeing. If the results are positive without an unacceptable loss of access, the scheme could be extended. However, any report should distinguish seasonal changes from effects plausibly linked to the new schedule. A review after three months would allow the organisation to revise the policy using comparable evidence instead of relying on isolated success stories.
